food.text: In 2025, Italian cuisine was listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. It is one of the best-known and most widely appreciated cuisines in the world. In 2024 it generated an estimated €251 billion in global foodservice revenue, according to Deloitte.

Carbonara, a pasta dish of cured pork, hard cheese, eggs, salt and black pepper, took its modern form and name in the middle of the 20th century. The names pasta alla carbonara and spaghetti alla carbonara are unrecorded before the Second World War. It is typical of the Lazio region.

In 2008, Italians were estimated to eat over 27 kg of pasta per person per year, easily beating Americans at about 9 kg. Because Italian pasta consumption exceeds the country's average wheat production, Italy frequently imports wheat for pasta making.

In 2018, Italy was the world's largest exporter of pasta, selling $2.9 billion worth, ahead of China with $0.9 billion. In 2015 to 2016, Italy was also the largest producer of dried pasta at 3.2 million tonnes, followed by the United States.

Neapolitan pizza was registered with the European Union as a traditional speciality guaranteed dish in 2009, at Italy's request. In 2017 the art of its making was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

Carbonara does not appear in Ada Boni's 1930 cookbook La cucina romana, and a major Italian cookbook published in 1950, Il cucchiaio d'argento, does not mention it either. Historians see this as supporting a post-World War II origin after the Allied liberation of Rome in 1944.

Apulia is a massive food producer, growing wheat, tomatoes, chickpeas, lentils and much more, and making cheeses such as caciocavallo and the famous burrata. It is also the largest producer of olive oil in Italy.
Up to 20% of the flour in a traditional pizza crust can be strong Manitoba flour. It was introduced to Italy from Canada as part of the Marshall Plan after World War II.

The name spaghetti alla carbonara first appeared in print in a 1939 Dutch East Indies newspaper, De Koerier, which mentioned a Trastevere restaurant in Rome known for it. In 1950, La Stampa reported that American officers had been seeking out the dish in Trastevere restaurants for years. Neither article described the dish.

The first attested carbonara recipe appeared in an illustrated cookbook published in Chicago in 1952 by Patricia Bronté. Luca Cesari writes that it was probably brought to the United States by an American serviceman or an Italian American who had encountered it in Rome. Alberto Grandi's claim that the first recipe is American has been criticized in Italy.

art.text: Italian Rationalism developed mostly in Italy in the 1920s and 1930s. It grew from a shared belief that the varied problems of the real world could be resolved by reason. It was a reaction against Historicism and a contrast to Art Nouveau and Expressionism.
Mussolini used several architectural styles, mixing classical elements into modern Rationalist architecture. The aim was to convey a sense of continuity with ancient Rome.
Rome's EUR district was chosen in the 1930s as the site of the 1942 World's Fair. Benito Mussolini planned it to celebrate twenty years of Fascism. The fair never took place because of World War II.

The Fascist architecture of EUR appeared prominently in Michelangelo Antonioni's 1962 film L'Eclisse and Bernardo Bertolucci's 1970 film The Conformist. Buildings there were also shown in Federico Fellini's 8½ and Boccaccio '70.

Italian Rationalism in architecture grew from a common belief that the most varied problems of the real world could be resolved by reason. It developed mostly in Italy in the 1920s and 1930s as a reaction to Historicism. Gruppo 7 mounted three exhibitions between 1926 and 1931.

Gruppo 7 mounted three exhibitions between 1926 and 1931, and the movement formed an official body, the Movimento Italiano per l'Architettura Razionale (MIAR), in 1930. Exemplary works include Giuseppe Terragni's Casa del Fascio in Como, built from 1932 to 1936.

The Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana, built from 1938 to 1943, is the most representative building at EUR. Known as the Colosseo Quadrato, or Square Colosseum, it was designed by Giovanni Guerrini, Ernesto Lapadula and Mario Romano, and was also inspired by metaphysical art.

The E42 project, born for the 1942 Rome Universal Expo, was meant to be a lasting example of a Mussolinian city, with buildings built to last hundreds if not thousands of years. Modern designs featuring glass skyscrapers were scrapped in favor of buildings with Roman elements, a city of arches and columns meant to convey the idea that "a people of conquerors and dominators had returned". The profits from the Expo were also to be used to finance the war, which was expected to begin after 1942 or 1945.
The Fascist regime that ruled Italy between 1922 and 1943 developed an architectural style linked to ancient Roman architecture. Its most important site in Rome is the E.U.R. district, built in 1935.

Rome's National Gallery of Modern Art displays works by Italian artists including Balla, Morandi, Carrà and De Chirico. In 2010, MAXXI, the National Museum of the 21st Century Arts, opened in a design by architect Zaha Hadid.

Giuseppe Pagano became editor of Casabella in 1933 together with Edoardo Persico. Their editorials urged the Italian state to adopt rationalism as its official style. The state instead tended to favor the more classically inspired work of the National Union of Architects.

In the late 1960s a new rationalist movement called the Tendenza emerged, centered in Italy. Its practitioners included Carlo Aymonino, Aldo Rossi and Giorgio Grassi. A Tendenza exhibition was organized for the 1973 Milan Triennale.
The E.U.R. district was conceived for a 1942 world exhibition and called E.42. The exhibition never took place because Italy entered the Second World War in 1940.

In 1930 the Italian Rationalists organized themselves as an official body, the Movimento Italiano per l'Architettura Razionale (MIAR). Pagano and Edoardo Persico later used the magazine Casabella to urge the Italian state to adopt rationalism as its official style.

In the 1950s in Italy, studies on rationalism and the methodology of science were developed in particular by Gualtiero Galmanini. He left an imprint that was later followed by many, influencing the starchitects of his time.

The Palace of Justice of Milan, built between 1932 and 1940, closely resembles the façades of the New Reich Chancellery, built in 1938 and 1939. The Milan tribunal is much bigger and more modern in style, and it is unclear whether it influenced the Chancellery's design.
The most representative Fascist-style building at E.U.R. is the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana, built between 1938 and 1943. Its iconic design has been labelled the cubic or Square Colosseum.

In the late 1960s a new rationalist movement, the Tendenza, emerged in Italy, claiming inspiration from both the Enlightenment and early-20th-century rationalists. Manfredo Tafuri became chair of Architecture History at the University Iuav of Venice in 1968, and it became a center of the movement. A Tendenza exhibition was organized for the 1973 Milan Triennale.

war.text: In the Italian campaign of World War II, Allied and Axis forces fought in and around Italy from 1943 to 1945. The Allies invaded Sicily in July 1943, then the Italian mainland in September, and the fighting lasted until the Axis forces in Italy surrendered in May 1945. Between September 1943 and April 1945, an estimated 60,000 to 70,000 Allied soldiers and between 38,805 and 150,660 German soldiers died in Italy. Over 150,000 Italian civilians died as well, and both sides committed war crimes.

Rome was bombed several times during 1943 and 1944, mostly by Allied aircraft and to a smaller degree by Axis aircraft. The city was liberated by the Allies on June 4, 1944. Vatican City was also caught up in the bombing, though it kept an official policy of neutrality.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: The Axis began as the Rome-Berlin Axis. After Germany and Italy signed a protocol in October 1936, Italian leader Benito Mussolini declared that all other European countries would rotate on the Rome-Berlin axis, creating the term. It became a military alliance in 1939 under the so-called Pact of Steel.

The invasion of Sicily in July 1943 led to the collapse of the Fascist Italian regime. King Victor Emmanuel III had Mussolini deposed and arrested on 25 July. The new government signed an armistice with the Allies on 8 September 1943.

On July 19, 1943, 690 United States Army Air Forces aircraft dropped 9,125 bombs on Rome. The raid targeted the freight yard and steel factory in the San Lorenzo district, but the bombs also struck the district's apartment blocks, damaging the Papal Basilica and killing 1,500 people.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: After the armistice, German forces invaded northern and central Italy and committed several atrocities against Italian civilians and army units who opposed the occupation, which started the Italian resistance movement. Research funded by the German government in 2016 found 22,000 victims of Nazi war crimes in Italy, mostly Italian civilians, sometimes killed in retaliation for partisan attacks, and Italian Jews. In the Marzabotto massacre over 770 civilians were murdered, and at Sant'Anna di Stazzema 560 were killed. Mussolini, rescued by German paratroopers, set up a puppet state called the Italian Social Republic to administer the occupied territory.

Pope Pius XII visited the bombed San Lorenzo district after the July 1943 raid. He had earlier asked President Roosevelt not to bomb Rome because of its value to the whole of humanity. Photographs of his visit later became a symbol of anti-war sentiments in Italy.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: Rome was declared an open city on August 14, 1943, by the defending Italian forces, a day after the last Allied bombing raid of that period. Pope Pius XII had earlier tried unsuccessfully to secure this status through negotiations with Roosevelt via Archbishop Francis Spellman.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: The Allied air campaign against Rome involved 110,000 sorties. In it, 600 aircraft were lost and 3,600 air crew members died. The Allies dropped 60,000 tons of bombs in the 78 days before they captured Rome on June 4, 1944.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: On 13 October 1943, the Allies recognized Italy as a co-belligerent against Germany. The Italian Co-Belligerent Army and the Italian partisans then fought alongside the Allies against German troops and the collaborationist National Republican Army. This aspect of the period is part of the Italian civil war.

Vichy French bombers based in North Africa raided the British base at Gibraltar during the Dakar fighting. About 50 aircraft dropped 150 bombs on 24 September, and about 100 aircraft dropped 300 bombs on 25 September on the harbour and dockyards. Most of the bombs missed, but some damage was caused and a few civilians were killed. The raid on 25 September also sank the British armed trawler HMT Stella Sirius.

Vatican City was bombed on at least two occasions during the war, on November 5, 1943, and March 1, 1944. Accounts differ on which side was responsible for each incident. The March 1944 bombing, by a British plane that dropped six bombs too close to the Vatican wall, killed a workman who was in the open and injured a Dutch Augustinian at the College of Saint Monica. The November 1943 bombing, in which a single plane dropped four bombs, caused no deaths.
war.source_title: Bombing of Rome in World War II

war.text: Northern Italy was liberated after a final spring offensive and a general insurrection of Italian partisans on 25 April 1945. Mussolini was captured by the Italian resistance and summarily executed by firing squad. The campaign ended when Army Group C surrendered unconditionally on 2 May 1945, one week before the formal German Instrument of Surrender. By then 35,828 anti-Nazi and anti-fascist partisans and some 35,000 troops of the Italian Social Republic had died.

literature.text: The Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded to Italian language authors six times as of 2019. Winners include Grazia Deledda, Luigi Pirandello, Salvatore Quasimodo, Eugenio Montale and Dario Fo.
Important early 20th century Italian writers include Giovanni Pascoli, Italo Svevo, Gabriele D'Annunzio, Umberto Saba, Giuseppe Ungaretti, Eugenio Montale and Luigi Pirandello.

Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa wrote only one novel, Il Gattopardo (The Leopard, 1958). It is nonetheless one of the most famous in Italian literature, and it deals with the life of a Sicilian nobleman in the 19th century.

Umberto Eco became internationally successful with Il nome della rosa (The Name of the Rose, 1980). The book is a Medieval detective story, and it made him one of the best-known Italian authors abroad.

Luigi Pirandello won the 1934 Nobel Prize in Literature. He explored the shifting nature of reality in his prose fiction and in plays such as Sei personaggi in cerca d'autore (Six Characters in Search of an Author, 1921).
tags: Six Characters in Search of an Author

literature.text: Italo Svevo, counted among the important early 20th century Italian writers, is the author of La coscienza di Zeno, published in 1923. It stands alongside the work of his contemporary Luigi Pirandello.
Leonardo Sciascia came to public attention with his novel Il giorno della civetta (The Day of the Owl, 1961). It exposed the extent of Mafia corruption in modern Sicilian society.

Neorealism was developed by Alberto Moravia, while Pier Paolo Pasolini became notable as one of the most controversial authors in the history of Italy. Both belong to the generation that shaped Italian writing after the early 20th century masters.

politics.text: Italy stopped recognising nobility when the Italian Republic was created in 1946. Many noble titles still exist, but they are used only as a social courtesy and have no standing under Italian law.

The House of Savoy ruled as Kings of Italy from 1861 to 1946. In the Mussolini years its crown also took in other titles: Emperors of Ethiopia (1936 to 1941), Kings of Albania (1939 to 1943) and Kings of Croatia (1941 to 1943).

In the aftermath of the First World War, most Italians who were ennobled received their titles through the patronage of the Mussolini government. Many were victory titles for services to the nation in the Great War, such as General Armando Diaz, who became Duca della Vittoria.

By the 20th century, new noble titles in Italy were nominated by the Prime Minister and approved by the Crown. Admiral Paolo Thaon di Revel was made Duca del Mare, and Commodore Luigi Rizzo became Conte di Grado e di Premuda.

In 1924 the writer and aviator Gabriele d'Annunzio was created Principe di Montenevoso. That same year the physicist, inventor and Nobel laureate Guglielmo Marconi was ennobled as Marchese Marconi, showing that Mussolini's government honoured cultural and scientific figures as well as soldiers.

Mussolini's government also ennobled its own leading figures. Costanzo Ciano became Conte di Cortellazzo i Buccari, Dino Grandi became Conte di Mordano, and Cesare Maria de Vecchi became Conte di Val Cismon. In 1937 Ettore Tolomei was made Conte della Vetta.

When Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli became Pope in 1939, Mussolini had the title of Principe posthumously bestowed on the new Pontiff's brother, Francesco Pacelli. Francesco had already been made a Marchese by the Holy See during his lifetime.

philosophy.text: The 25th World Congress of Philosophy took place in Rome in August 2024. These global gatherings of philosophers are held every five years under the International Federation of Philosophical Societies (FISP). The series was first organized in 1900.

Religion in Italy has long been shaped by the dominance of the Catholic Church. The 2018 Eurobarometer survey showed that 85.6% of Italy's population was Christian, including 78.9% Catholics. Another 11.7% were non-religious, made up of 7.5% atheists and 4.2% agnostics.

A 2005 Eurobarometer poll asked Italians about belief. It found that 74% believed there is a God, and 16% believed in some sort of spirit or life force. Only 6% did not believe in any sort of spirit, God, or life force.

Italy hosted a philosophy gathering early in this era. After the first congresses, the International Congress of Philosophy met in Naples in 1924, followed by Cambridge, US in 1926 and Oxford, UK in 1930. The event became known as the World Congress of Philosophy only in 1973.

Surveys of Italian religiosity do not always move in one direction. Eurispes found that Catholics fell from 87.8% of Italian citizens in 2006 to 71.1% in 2016. Yet religious practice, which had fallen to 24.4% by 2010, rose slightly to 25.4% by 2016.

Italy was the only country in the 2017 Pew survey Being Christian in Western Europe that had more practising Christians than non-practising ones. In that survey, 58% of Italians considered religion very or somewhat important.

culture.text: Football is the most popular sport in Rome, as in the rest of Italy. The city hosted the final games of the 1934 and 1990 FIFA World Cup, the latter at the Stadio Olimpico.
Italy's Scuderia Ferrari is the oldest surviving team in Grand Prix racing, having competed since 1948. It is statistically the most successful Formula One team in history, with a record of 232 wins.

Rome is widely recognized as a world fashion capital. According to the 2009 Global Language Monitor, it is the world's 4th most important fashion center, after Milan, New York City and Paris, and ahead of London.

Catholicism has long dominated religion in Italy, yet practice has been falling. According to ISTAT data, the proportion of Italians who have never practiced a religion doubled from 16% in 2001 to 31% in 2022.

A.S. Roma and S.S. Lazio share the Stadio Olimpico, and their rivalry has become a staple of Roman sports culture. Locally born footballers such as Francesco Totti and Daniele De Rossi, both of A.S. Roma, tend to become especially popular.

Rome's fashion scene includes major luxury houses such as Bulgari, Fendi, Valentino, Laura Biagiotti and Brioni, which are headquartered or were founded in the city. Labels such as Chanel, Prada and Armani have boutiques along the upscale Via dei Condotti.

The Italian Grand Prix of Formula 1 has been held since 1921, making it the fifth oldest surviving Grand Prix. Every Formula 1 Grand Prix except for the 1980 one has been held at Autodromo Nazionale Monza.

The 20th Rome Film Festival's official poster was a shot by Franco Pinna, taken on the set of Federico Fellini's 1965 film Juliet of the Spirits. The festival celebrated the birth centenary of Pinna, an Italian photographer of the second half of the 20th century.
